(2018)) with key characters of two to four locules, two to four styles, entire stipules, male flowers with four tepals, palmate or palmate-pinnate venation and axillary inflorescences. The most similar species to B. dicressine in the area seems to be B. rockii, distributed in Chinese Yunnan and north east Myanmar. B. rockii shares several characters with B. dicressine, including being a low growing plant lacking erect stems, leaf shape, iridescence and number of tepals in the male flowers (Cuizhi et al. 2007). However, Begonia dicressine differs in several critical characters such as sparsely hairy petioles, the glabrous leaf surface, inflorescence
bibliographic_Citation: Wahlsteen E. 2019, A new species of Begonia L. (Begoniaceae) and some notes on Begonia difformis from Kachin, northern Myanmar, Phytotaxa. Vol.420(3) , pp.241-248 (https://doi.org/10.11646/phytotaxa.420.3.4)

description: Low growing caulescent herbs, monoecious; stems repent or suberect and adventitiously rooting at the nodes. Leaves alternate, ovate to lanceolate, finely divided or entire. Inflorescences terminal or axillary, cymose, bracts conspicuous, usually persistent, white or pink. Male flowers basal, tepals 3–4, in unequal pairs or one tepal reduced, free, white, stamens 4–8, free, androecium symmetric. Female flowers solitary, terminal, tepals 3–4, in unequal pairs or one tepal reduced, free, white or pink, styles bifid and branched or capitate and cylindrical, not spirally twisted. Fruit 3-locular, placentae axillary, bifid; wings 3, unequal (1+2), fleshy and horn-like, the larger wing extended apically towards the tepals, smaller wings rounded.Taxonomic notes:—The affinities of Begonia sect. Oligandrae are difficult to ascertain, primarily because the reproductive structures are unusual and highly modified. Reduced stamen number and showy bracts are similarly found in Begonia sect. Symbegonia (Warburg 1894: 149) Forrest& Hollingsworth (2003: 208) endemic to New Guinea and possibly the closest relative to the new section. However sect. Symbegonia differs (corresponding characters for sect. Oligandrae in parentheses) in usually having solitary-axillary female flowers (female flowers inserted at the apex of a male cymose inflorescence in B. pentandra and B. chambersiae), fused female tepals (free female tepals), noticeably enlarged receptacles (planate or slightly rounded receptacles), and elongated stigmas (stigmas inconspicuous or capitate). Repeated attempts at DNA-sequencing from silica dried leaves of B. sandsiana and B. pentandra were unsuccessful, hence the phylogenetic relationship of the new section remains unknown.
bibliographic_Citation: Hughes M. & Takeuchi W.N. 2015, A new section (Begonia sect. Oligandrae sect. nov.) and a new species (Begonia pentandra sp. nov.) in Begoniaceae from New Guinea, Phytotaxa. Vol.197(1) , pp.037-044 (http://dx.doi.org/10.11646/phytotaxa.197.1.4)

description: Begonia truncatifolia is immediately unique from most Begonia section Baryandra by having spathulate leaves. The species is most similar to B. blancii in having spathulate leaves, 4-tepaled staminate and pistillate flowers, and bilocular ovaries. However, B. truncatifolia is different in having smaller stipules (8–10 mm × 4–5mm vs. ca. 15 mm × 12 mm); sub-rhomboidal to obtriangularoblong lamina (vs. obtriangular-spathulate) with obtusely rounded to acute apex (vs. broad, truncate or with shallow round lobes); and minute sparse pilose inflorescence (vs. with scattered long pale hairs).Notes:—The majority of the population of Begonia truncatifolia observed show a high degree of variegation on their leaves, varying from brown mottled patches to white/silvery streaks (Figs. 3& 4). Other individuals observed are plain green and devoid of the patches and streaks. The new species is the second Begonia species in the Philippines known to have truncate, spathulate leaves, after Begonia blancii, which is also its most similar species. A comparison of the two species is enumerated in Table 1. They are both endemic to the island of Palawan and are only known from their respective type localities, which are at least 70 km apart (Figure 1).
contributor: Bustamante R.A.A., Tandang D.N., Pranada M.A.K. & Ang Y.P.
bibliographic_Citation: Bustamante R.A.A., Tandang D.N., Pranada M.A.K. & Ang Y.P. 2020, Begonia truncatifolia (Begoniaceae, section Baryandra), a new species from Palawan Island, the Philippines, Phytotaxa. Vol.458(3) , pp.215-222 (https://doi.org/10.11646/phytotaxa.458.3.4)

description: Notes This is one of the most easily recognisable sections of Begonia in the Americas, comprising caulescent species with highly distinctive 3-horned fruits that dehisce dorsally rather than laterally as in most begonias. This character was also shared with B. sect. Semibegoniella (C.DC.) F.A.Barkley& Baranov, whose species differed in their fused tepals, but this section was recently brought into synonymy with B. sect. Casparya based upon evidence from molecular phylogenies (Jara-Muñoz et al. 2019). Begonia sect. Casparya is most diverse in the northern Andes of Ecuador and Colombia. We recognise three species from Peru including one new species and two endemics.
bibliographic_Citation: Moonlight P.W. et al. 2023, The genus Begonia (Begoniaceae) in Peru, Eur. J. Taxon. Vol.881 , pp.1-334 (https://doi.org/10.5852/ejt.2023.881.2175)

description: The new species is most similar to B. tatianae Aver. in Averyanov et al. (2019a: 93), differing mainly in its leaves with hairy petiole and blade, adaxial surface of blade with numerous irregular spots and without crystalloid bodies, inflorescences 2.5–8 cm long and as long as leaves, pistillate flowers with 5 tepals, glabrous ovary.Notes:—The new species is tentatively placed in Begonia subg. Petermannia (Klotzsch 1854: 124) Y.M.Shui& W.H.Chen in Shui et al. (2019b: 141) on the basis of its creeping rhizomes and zygomorphic androecium, because this combination of characters is common among the species of this subgenus (Shui et al. 2019b). In particular, B. aspersa is morphologically close to a number of representatives of B. sect. Petermannia within the expanded circumscription of the section proposed by Shui et al. (2019b). In having stemless rhizomatous habit, B. aspersa is similar to some species from the Philippines and China (Taiwan) formerly recognized within B. sect. Baryandra de Candolle (1859: 122) (currently synonymized with sect. Petermannia; Shui et al. 2019b), such as B. fenicis Merrill (1908: 421).
bibliographic_Citation: Averyanov L. et al. 2021, New and noteworthy species of Begonia (Begoniaceae) from Vietnam and Laos , Phytotaxa. Vol.522(2) , pp.075-093 (https://doi.org/10.11646/phytotaxa.522.2.1)

description: Similar to B. rubrosetosa Aver. in Averyanov& Nguyen (2012: 20) and B. saolaensis Y.M.Shui, T.A.Le& C.T.Vu in Shui et al. (2019a: 61), differing in glabrous stem, petiole, leaf blade, pedicel and ovary, stipules 4–8 × 1.5–3 mm, narrowly oblong-lanceolate leaf blade, tepals of staminate flowers 2–3.5 mm long, tepals of pistillate flowers 3–4.5 mm long and abaxially hairy, styles 1 mm long.Notes:—Begonia gracilifolia is similar to B. rubrosetosa and B. saolaensis in having lanceolate or ovate leaf blade, outer tepals of staminate flowers abaxially with red hairs, emarginate apex of anthers, and ovary with three subequal wings. These morphological characteristics indicate that B. gracilifolia, together with the two latter species, is a member of B. sect. Petermannia (Moonlight et al. 2018, Shui et al. 2019b). Begonia gracilifolia differs from B. rubrosetosa (Averyanov& Nguyen 2012, Hughes et al. 2018) in stipules 4–8 × 1.5–3 (vs. 5–15 × 3–10) mm, narrowly oblong-lanceolate (vs. narrowly ovate) leaf blade, glabrous (vs. glabrous to sparsely pubescent) pedicel, tepals of staminate flowers 2–3.5 (vs. 3.5–9) mm long, tepals of pistillate flowers 3–4.5 (vs. 5–7) mm long, glabrous (vs. sparsely setose) ovary, and styles 1 (vs. 1.5–2.5) mm long. The new species differs from B. saolaensis in glabrous (vs. sparsely strigose) stem, stipules 4–8 × 1.5–3 (vs. 15–17 × 5–6) mm, glabrous (vs. strigose) petiole, narrowly oblong-lanceolate and glabrous (vs. ovate or broadly ovate and hairy) leaf blade, adaxially flat (vs. impressed) secondary veins of leaf blade, tepals of staminate flowers 2–3.5 (vs. 4–8) mm long, tepals of pistillate flowers abaxially hairy (vs. glabrous) and 3–4.5 (vs. 4–8) mm long.
bibliographic_Citation: Averyanov L. et al. 2021, New and noteworthy species of Begonia (Begoniaceae) from Vietnam and Laos , Phytotaxa. Vol.522(2) , pp.075-093 (https://doi.org/10.11646/phytotaxa.522.2.1)

description: Similar to B. duclouxii Gagnepain (1919: 198), B. limprichtii Irmsch. in Limpricht (1922: 440) and B. setifolia Irmscher (1939: 549), differing from them by the following combination of characters: leaf blade 8.2–11.5 cm long, hairy peduncle, bracts 3.5–5 mm long, purple tepals, staminate flowers with outer tepals ca. 6 mm long and ca. 3–4 mm wide, actinomorphic androecium, anthers with supraconnective.Notes:—Begonia maculifolia is most similar to B. duclouxii, B. limprichtii and B. setifolia (incl. B. tsaii Irmscher [1951: 42]) belonging to B. sect. Platycentrum (Shui et al. 2019b). The differences of the new species from B. duclouxii are: abaxially hairy stipules (vs. stipules glabrous, with apical setae), leaf blade 8.2–11.5 (vs. 4–8) cm long, sparsely hairy (vs. glabrous or subglabrous) peduncle, bracts 3.5–5 (vs. 9–11) mm long, mostly purple (vs. purely white) tepals, staminate flowers with outer tepals ca. 6 (vs. 11–15) mm long and ca. 3–4 (vs. 8–12) mm wide, anthers with supraconnective (vs. with emarginate apex) (Gagnepain 1919, Irmscher 1939, Gu et al. 2007, Shui& Chen 2017). It differs from B. limprichtii in staminate flowers with outer tepals ca. 6 (vs. 11–20) mm long and ca. 3–4 (vs. 6–15) mm wide, anthers with supraconnective (vs. with emarginate apex), pistillate flowers with outer tepals 12 (vs. 15–16) mm long (Limpricht 1922, Gu et al. 2007, Shui& Chen 2017, Hughes et al. 2018, Borah et al. 2021). The new species differs from B. setifolia in abaxially hairy (vs. glabrous, with apical setae) stipules, inflorescence bracts 3.5–5 (vs. 4–10) mm long and ca. 1.5–2 (vs. 2.4–8) mm wide, staminate flowers with outer tepals ca. 6 (vs. 16–22) mm long and ca. 3–4 (vs. 16–18) mm wide, actinomorphic (vs. zygomorphic) androecium, anthers with supraconnective (vs. with emarginate apex), pistillate flowers with 2 (vs. 2 or 3) styles (Irmscher 1939, 1951, Gu et al. 2007, Shui& Chen 2017). In addition, B. maculifolia shares with B. tamdaoensis C.I Peng in Peng et al. (2015: 94), another member of B. sect. Platycentrum, a set of characters including creeping rhizome, ovate leaf blade, stamen filaments extended to supraconnectives and presumably bilocular ovary. The new species differs from B. tamdaoensis in absence of aerial stem (vs. presence during anthesis), leaf blade with dark patches (vs. uniformly green) and adaxially hairy (vs. glabrous or subglabrous), actinomorphic (vs. zygomorphic) androecium of ca. 100 (vs. 12–35) stamens, and 2 (vs. 3) styles (Peng et al. 2015, Hughes et al. 2018). Finally, the new species shows some similarity with B. versicolor Irmscher (1939: 546) in habit, hairy adaxial surface of leaf blade and presumably bilocular ovary, but can be readily distinguished by its stipules 4–9 × 3–4 (vs. 8–9 × 5–8) mm, outer tepals of pistillate flowers abaxially with several hairs (vs. villous), and 2 (vs. 3) styles (Gu et al. 2007, Shui& Chen 2017, Hughes et al. 2018, and see below).
bibliographic_Citation: Averyanov L. et al. 2021, New and noteworthy species of Begonia (Begoniaceae) from Vietnam and Laos , Phytotaxa. Vol.522(2) , pp.075-093 (https://doi.org/10.11646/phytotaxa.522.2.1)

description: Note:—The species is reported here from Vietnam for the first time
bibliographic_Citation: Averyanov L. et al. 2021, New and noteworthy species of Begonia (Begoniaceae) from Vietnam and Laos , Phytotaxa. Vol.522(2) , pp.075-093 (https://doi.org/10.11646/phytotaxa.522.2.1)

description: Notes:—The presence of this species in Vietnam is confirmed here by specimen citation for the first time. Li et al. (2018) treated B. versicolor as a narrow endemic of southeast Yunnan. Hughes et al. (2015–, 2018) indicated B. versicolor to inhabit northern Vietnam, and Pham et al. (2021) listed it for the country, but they have not provided any documentation of their records.
bibliographic_Citation: Averyanov L. et al. 2021, New and noteworthy species of Begonia (Begoniaceae) from Vietnam and Laos , Phytotaxa. Vol.522(2) , pp.075-093 (https://doi.org/10.11646/phytotaxa.522.2.1)

description: Remarkable in producing bulbils at junction of petiole and leaf blade; most close to B. longialata K.Y.Guan& D.K.Tian (2000: 132), differing in petiole 5–10 cm long, shallowly lobed leaf blade 8–12 cm long and wide and setose on both sides and margin, staminate flowers with pedicel 12–22 mm long and tepals subequal in length, pistillate flowers with pedicel 0.4–1.2 cm long and with 4 tepals, styles 2.2–3 mm long. Also the new species is similar to B. macrotoma Irmscher (1951: 41), differing in its abaxially hairy leaf blade, glabrous peduncle, abaxially glabrous outer tepals of staminate flowers and all tepals of pistillate flowers, staminate flowers with outer tepals 10–15 mm long and 16–21 mm wide, pistillate flowers with 2 or 3 styles.Notes:—Begonia vivipara is placed in B. sect. Platycentrum on the basis of its thick rhizome and bicarpellate gynoecium (Moonlight et al. 2018, Shui et al. 2019b). Within this section, the new species is morphologically most close to B. longialata (Guan& Tian 2000, Shui& Chen 2017, Hughes et al. 2018), but differs in shorter floriferous stem 14–27 (vs. 30–50) cm long, shorter petiole 5–10 (vs. 13–31) cm long, leaf blade broadly ovate (vs. ovate), 8–12 cm long and wide (vs. 24–44 cm long, 24–41 cm wide), shallowly lobed, not more than to 1/3 of leaf length (vs. deeply lobed, more than to 2/3 of leaf length), setose on both sides and leaf margin (vs. entirely glabrous), regularly with small bulbils at the base (vs. without bulbils), long peduncles to 20 (vs. 5–10) cm long, staminate flowers with pedicel 12–22 (vs. 2–5) mm long and tepals subequal in length (vs. inner tepals distinctly shorter than the outer ones), pistillate flowers with pedicel 0.4–1.2 cm long, elongating in fruit to 2.5 cm and normally with 4 tepals (vs. pedicel 1.8–4.8 cm long and normally 5 tepals), short styles 2.2–3 (vs. 4.2–4.8) mm long, capsules 1.2–2.2 (vs. about 1.6) cm long, with larger wing 2.8–4.2 (vs. 3–5) cm wide.
bibliographic_Citation: Averyanov L. et al. 2021, New and noteworthy species of Begonia (Begoniaceae) from Vietnam and Laos , Phytotaxa. Vol.522(2) , pp.075-093 (https://doi.org/10.11646/phytotaxa.522.2.1)

description: Notes: Begonia villosula resembles B. thomsonii A.DC. (1859: 134), which belongs to the same section and also occurs in Indochine. The two species are similar in their ovate, hairy leaves and hairy inflorescence arising directly from a short aerial stem, yet B. villosula differs from B. thomsonii (Fig. 4) in its leaves’ upper surface with minutely raised cones topped (vs. relatively flat), a white hirsute (vs. villous) top, leaf margins crenate to crenulate (vs. entire with teeth at end of veins to denticulate), stamens 80–120 (vs. 35–70), pistillate flower 4-tepaled (vs. 5-tepaled) and ovary hirsute (vs. villous). In its hairy foliage, 4-tepaled staminate flower and 5-tepaled flower, ovary 2-loculate with three unequal wings. Begonia villosula also resembles B. villifolia Irmsch. (1951: 43). However, the new species is clearly distinct from B. villifolia in its aerial stems being seen only at anthesis (vs. persistent), stem shorter (up to ca. 10 cm vs. to 80 cm), leaf margins crenate to crenulate (vs. irregularly serrate) and unlobed (vs. shallowly lobed), stamens 80–120 (vs. ca. 400). A comparison of the salient characters of the three species is presented in Table 1.
bibliographic_Citation: Hoang T.S. & Lin C-W. 2021, Two new species of Begonia (sect. Platycentrum, Begoniaceae) from the Central Highlands of Vietnam: B. villosula and B. lophura, Phytotaxa. Vol.510(3) , pp.263-274 (https://doi.org/10.11646/phytotaxa.510.3.6)

description: Notes: Begonia lophura resembles B. pavonina Ridley (1909: 22), while the latter is a handsome species from Cameron Highlands in Peninsular Malaysia and also belongs to sect. Platycentrum. The two species bear superficial similarities by having ovate leaves that have upper surfaces which produce an indigo blue iridescence when the light is reflected at certain angles, 4-tepaled staminate flower and 5-tepaled pistillate flower. However, B. lophura is distinct from B. pavonina (Fig. 7) in its leaves that are widely ovate (vs. ovate) and red hirsute on abaxial surface (vs. glabrous), bracts persistent (vs. caducous), tepals hirsute in both of staminate and pistillate flowers (vs. glabrous), capsule scabrous (vs. glabrous) and abaxial wing strongly swollen (vs. thin, not swollen). The new species is also closely similar to B. menglianensis Y.Y. Qian (2001:461) in widely ovate, velvety foliage and inflorescence structure, but differs in its adaxial lamina surface with blue iridescence (vs. absence of blue iridescence), ovary hirsute (vs. fusco-villose) and abaxial wing strongly swollen (vs. thin, not swollen). A comparison of the three phonetically similar species is presented in Table 2.
bibliographic_Citation: Hoang T.S. & Lin C-W. 2021, Two new species of Begonia (sect. Platycentrum, Begoniaceae) from the Central Highlands of Vietnam: B. villosula and B. lophura, Phytotaxa. Vol.510(3) , pp.263-274 (https://doi.org/10.11646/phytotaxa.510.3.6)

description: Notes:—The collection chosen as the neotype is a very good match for the original description, in which Jack (1822) writes “The flowers come in fascicles from the middle of the petioles, and these flower bearing leaves are always opposed to another without flowers; hence it is that the upper leaves are opposite, while the lower are alternate.” This morphology is illustrated nicely in Fig 1A, however what Jack considered to be a petiole with an inflorescence is much better interpreted as short sympodial branch off the main stem.
bibliographic_Citation: Girmansyah D. & et. al. 2020, A key to Begonia section Bracteibegonia from Sumatra with one new species and rediscovery of Begonia fasciculata Jack, Phytotaxa. Vol.475(4) , pp.289-295 (https://doi.org/10.11646/phytotaxa.475.4.6)

description: The new species is similar to B. namkadingensis C. J. Yang, Souladeth& Tagane (Yang et al. 2018: 195) in its tuberous habit, and tepal number of the male and female flower, but significantly differs by its more stamens (20–25 vs. 4–7), 3 (vs. 2) stigmas, and 3-locular (vs. 2-locular) ovary. Begonia depingiana also resembles B. pellionioides in having pinnate leaf venation, but differs by its shorter plant (5−25 cm vs. up to 80 cm), tuberous rootstock (vs. rhizomatous), densely pinkish-white ciliate (vs. glabrous) ovary. Comparison of the above three species is provided in Table 1.Note:—Begonia depingiana has tuberous habit, alternate leaves, 3 stigmas, 3-locular ovary and bifid placenta. In Begonia sect. Pteridiformis Y.M. Shui& W.H. Chen (Shui et al. 2019: 190), only two species, B. namkadingensis and B. pteridiformis Phutthai (Phutthai& Sridith 2010: 37), have 2 stigmas and 2-locular fruits with one enlarged wing. So, we tentatively classify this species in sect. Pteridiformis Y.M. Shui& W.H. Chen (Shui et al. 2019: 190) based on the morphology. Further studies would be necessary to clarify its taxonomic status.
bibliographic_Citation: Ding H.B., et al. 2020, A new tuberous species of Begonia L. (Begoniaceae) from southern Yunnan, China, Phytotaxa. Vol.474(1) , pp.081-086 (https://doi.org/10.11646/phytotaxa.474.1.8)

description: Begonia margaretiana is closely related to Begonia paulensis de Candolle (1859:125) but can be distinguished by erect plant vs. rhizomatous, stipules falcate vs. triangular, leaves not peltate vs. peltate, larger capsule wing 1.4–2 cm vs. 2–2.5 cm wide, capsule glabrous vs. strigose
bibliographic_Citation: Kollmann L.J.C. 2020, NOVELTIES IN BRAZILIAN BEGONIACEAE III: Begonia margaretiana, a new species from Rio de Janeiro state, Phytotaxa. Vol.466(1) , pp.72-76 (https://doi.org/10.11646/phytotaxa.466.1.9)

description: B. beijnenii is most allied to B. hughesii by bearing 3-winged ovary with a cucullate wing and an abortive abaxial locule, petiole vestiture tormentose, leaf glabrous adaxially and subglabrous abaxially. However, Begonia beijnenii is distinctively different in being comparatively smaller in size. B. beijnenii differs from B. hughesii (differences in parentheses) by having rhizome 3–4 mm in diameter (vs 5–10 mm in diameter), internodes of 2–2.5 mm (vs 3–8 mm), stipules glabrous except keel has ca. 1 or none straight hair near the attachment (vs dimorphic character: brown hairs on keel only or tormentose entirely abaxially), leaf lamina subrhomboid, 4.1–4.8 × 3.8–4.6 cm (vs ovate, 7–10 × 5–7.5 cm), peduncle length 6–9.6 cm (vs 15 cm), bracts glabrous, 4.5 × 3.5 mm in size (vs minute scattered glandular hairs, 1.5–2 × 1.5–2 mm in size), stamen count 22–32 (vs. ca. 40), ovary length 6–8 mm (vs 10 mm), cucullate wing 6–8 × 4–7 mm in size (vs 9–14 × 7–9 mm in size). Both species are only known from their type locality and vicinity, which is at least 40 km apart. Two other Palawan species: B. cleopatrae and B. gironellae also superficially resemble B. beijnenii by having a variegated leaf adaxial surface. A quick comparison is also provided to aid in identification (Table 1).Notes:—From the observations of authors, most Palawan Begonia of section Baryandra bears ovary with an underdeveloped or abortive abaxial locule. In addition, mottle maculation seems to be very common among species of section Baryandra. Recent surveys by authors in Palawan has also revealed an undocumented subpopulation of B. hughesii with mottle maculation (Figure 5).
contributor: Ang Y.P., Tandang D.N., Rubite R. & Bustamante R.A.A.
bibliographic_Citation: Ang Y.P., Tandang D.N., Rubite R. & Bustamante R.A.A. 2020, Begonia beijnenii (Begoniaceae, section Baryandra), a new species of Begonia from San Vicente, Palawan, the Philippines, Phytotaxa. Vol.455(3) , pp.196-204 (https://doi.org/10.11646/phytotaxa.455.3.2)

description: The new species is most similar to B. albopunctata Chen et al. (2018a: 66) in its broadly ovate leaves; red and 4- loculed ovary with three free styles; 2-lobed stigmas with twisted band; and red, berry-like fruits with a beaked apex, but differs principally in its glabrous abaxial leaf surface (vs. densely red pubescent), 1.8–2 cm long peduncle (vs. 6–9 cm), 2.5–4 cm long pedicels of staminate flower (vs. 0.5–1.5 cm), puberulous outer surface of tepals (vs. almost glabrous), 1.8–2 cm long pedicels of pistillate flower (vs. 0.4–0.7 cm), six tepals of pistillate flower (vs. five), and obovate or turbinate, wingless, and puberulous fruits (vs. rhomboid, four thickened rib-like horns, and densely white papillose).
contributor: Do T.V., Luu A.N.D. & Dong W-K.
bibliographic_Citation: Do T.V., Luu A.N.D. & Dong W-K. 2020, Begonia tadungensis (Begonia sect. Platycentrum), a new species from southern Vietnam, Phytotaxa. Vol.449(1) , pp.65-74 (https://doi.org/10.11646/phytotaxa.449.1.6)

description: Begonia vasconcelosiana is closely related to Begonia lealii Brade (1954: 81) in its peltate leaves, stellate trichomes, persistent stipules and bracts, and having prophylls, but can be distinguished from B. lealii by the petioles being 1.2–7.5 cm long (vs.1–2 cm), the inflorescence being 15–35 cm long (vs. 4–7 cm), bracts 3–6.5 × 1.2–3 mm (vs. 8–10 × 3–4 mm), the largest wing on the capsule being 8–9 mm and ascendant (vs. 1–2 mm long and not ascendant) and the other two wings being 5–7 mm long (vs.1 mm); also the internodes are much more congested in B. vasconcelosiana (to 1 cm long) than in B. lealii (to 5 cm long).
bibliographic_Citation: Kollmann L.J.C. 2020, NOVELTIES IN BRAZILIAN BEGONIACEAE II: a new species from Minas Gerais, Phytotaxa. Vol.437(3) , pp.156-160 (https://doi.org/10.11646/phytotaxa.437.3.4)

description: The new species is most allied to B. suborbiculata in producing suborbicular leaves, having a 5- winged ovary and a bilocular ovary, 2 placentae per locule, trichomes on outer surface of the tepals. In our analysis, we compared B. cabanillasii to two distinctive variants of B. suborbiculata. The morphological descriptions of B. suborbiculata was made based upon Lectotype descriptions of the species (Hughes et. al 2010) and the examination of specimen deposited in PNH (Rubite 352). Further characteristics not available in literatures and herbarium specimen were directly observed from living plants in the habitat. One of the variants has variegated leaves and erect short hirsute on the leaf adaxial (Rubite 352), deposited in PNH; photographed plants were from same locality and variant synonymous to the specimen observed. (to be referred to as B. suborbiculata 1) (Figure 4). The second variant was observed at Lake Manguao, Taytay, Palawan, with a glabrous leaf adaxial (to be referred to as B. suborbiculata 2)The two species are endemic to the island of Palawan. However, B. cabanillasii is distinct from both variants of B. suborbiculata in the following ways (the differences are presented in Figure 6& 7 and Table 1). For B. cabanillasii, the internodes are more comparatively compact at 2–4 mm long (vs. up to ca. 3 cm long in B. suborbiculata 1& 2); The lamina is thickly chartaceous (vs. fleshy) and non-waxy (vs. waxy); Leaf adaxial vestiture is pilose with white trichomes 2–2.5 mm long (vs. sparse hirsute with white trichomes ca. 1 mm long in B. suborbiculata 1; glabrous in B. suborbiculata 2); The lamina margin is shallowly undulating, ciliate with soft white trichomes ca. 1.5 mm long (vs. entire and minutely ciliate with brown trichomes ca. 0.5 mm long); stipules abaxial surface, upper-half is pilose with white trichomes and glabrescent (vs abaxial surface persistent brown puberulous); panicle length 9–15 cm long (vs. ca. 25 cm long). Begonia cabanillasii also has a comparatively larger inflorescence, with staminate flowers: pedicel 1.5–2.5 cm long (vs ca. 1 cm), outer tepal elliptic, 10–14 × 9–11.5 mm (vs orbicular, ca. 8 × 8 mm), inner tepal length 10–12 mm long (vs. ca. 8 mm long).Notes:—Begonia cabanillasii is a very decorative species. All plants observed bear variegation on its leaves, varying in the coverage of the black patches, with some individuals donned entirely black with only a silver streak down the midvein. Not only does it bear very unique and ornamental variegation on its leaves, it will be the third Begonia species in the Philippines known to have a 5-winged ovary; after B. quinquealata C.-I Peng, Rubite& C.W.Lin, and B. suborbiculata.
contributor: Ang Y.P., Tandang D.N., Agcaoili J. & Bustamante R.A.A.
bibliographic_Citation: Ang Y.P., Tandang D.N., Agcaoili J. & Bustamante R.A.A. 2020, Begonia cabanillasii (section Baryandra, Begoniaceae), a new species from El Nido, Palawan, the Philippines, Phytotaxa. Vol.453(3) , pp.244-254 (https://doi.org/10.11646/phytotaxa.453.3.6)

description: B. sidolensis is a species from montane forest of Gunung Sidole, Sulawesi. It resembles Begonia gemella Warb. ex Smith& Wasshausen (1983: 443), known from lowland limestone forests of Sulawesi, in the creeping habit and small lamina size, but can be easily distinguished by its shorter petioles (0.5–2vs 3−10 cm), male inflorescences comprised of 2−3 monochasial partial inflorescences with caducous bracteoles (vs male inflorescence a monochasium, bracteoles persistent), shorter male flower pedicels (13–16 vs 20–35 mm) and larger male flower tepals (11–13 × 14–15 vs 5–9 × 9–12 mm), and solitary female flowers with 5 tepals (vs female flowers 2-tepalled and usually paired with a single male flower).Notes:—Begonia sidolensis is an understorey herb that grows on steep slopes. The prostrate-creeping habit is a rare character in Begonia section Petermannia, although some other species with this growth habit are known from Sulawesi and the Moluccas (Sulawesi: B. gemella Warb. ex Sm.& Wassh.; B. flacca Irmscher (1953a: 486), B. mattampensis Ardi& D.C. Thomas (2019:23); Moluccas: B. manuselaensis Ardhaka& Ardi (Ardhaka et al. 2016: 61)). Apart from similarities to B. gemella (see diagnosis), B. sidolensis also has morphological similarities with B. manuselaensis, a creeping species described from lowland limestone forest from Seram, but B. sidolensis can be easily distinguished by stems and leaves that have a sparse indumentum of simple hairs or are glabrescent (vs a very sparse indumentum of small flattened red scales), shorter petioles (0.5–2 vs 4−7.5 cm), shorter male flower pedicels (1.3−1.6 vs. 4−7 cm) and shorter female flower pedicels (0.5−0.7 vs 1.5−4 cm). Begonia flacca and B. mattampensis are other allied species from Sulawesi, similar in their creeping habit, but B. sidolensis differs in having a much smaller stature. Further, both B. flacca and B. mattampensis are found in lowland limestone karst habitats and have never been reported from high altitudes.
contributor: Dayanti E.P., Pitopang R., Ardi W.H., & Thomas D.C.
bibliographic_Citation: Dayanti E.P., Pitopang R., Ardi W.H., & Thomas D.C. 2020, Two New Species of Begonia (Begoniaceae, Section Petermannia) from Mount Sidole, Central Sulawesi, Indonesia, Phytotaxa. Vol.439(2) , pp.136-142 (https://doi.org/10.11646/phytotaxa.439.2.4)

description: The species is closely related to Begonia dipetala Graham but differs in having tuberous roots (vs rhizomatous), the presence of axillary tubercles or cormlets (vs absence in all other Indian species), ovate bracts with obtuse apexes (vs triangular or ovate with acute apexes), 2 broadly orbicular tepals in the male and female flowers, which are 22–25 × 23–26 mm (vs tepals 2–(3) broadly ovate with obtuse apexes, which are 8–10 x 8–10 mm), 50–55 stamens (vs 30 stamens), ovaries with 3 unequal wings (vs ovaries with 3 equal wings), and luneate stigmas (vs reniform stigmas).
contributor: Aitawade M.M., Bachulkar M.Y. & Yadav S.
bibliographic_Citation: Aitawade M.M., Bachulkar M.Y. & Yadav S. 2019, Begonia handibadaganathensis (Begoniaceae), a new species from Western Ghats, India, Phytotaxa. Vol.423(3) , pp.206-210 (https://doi.org/10.11646/phytotaxa.423.3.9)

description: Begonia fimbritepala is most similar to B. olsoniae Smith& Schubert (1965: 250) but differs in having glabrous leaves on the adaxial surface, villous abaxial veins, with simple trichomes (vs. hispid on both surfaces, squamulose abaxial veins, fimbriate scales) and tepals with ciliate margins (vs entire to slightly crenulate).Taxonomic notes:— Begonia fimbritepala can be easily recognized by its combination of transversely ovate blades, glabrous on the adaxial leaf surface, apart from being villous with simple trichomes near the petiole, villous with simple trichomes along the principal veins on the abaxial leaf surface, and by having very long (1–1.5 mm) trichomes on the margins of tepals of the male and female flowers. This species resembles B. olsoniae by its rupicolous habit, transversely ovate leaf blades and size of male flowers. Begonia fimbritepala, however, has glabrous leaves on the adaxial surface, except by being villous nearest the petiole, villous abaxial veins, with simple trichomes (vs. hispid on both surface, squamulose abaxial veins, fimbriate scales), villous petioles (vs. squamulose), stipules glabrous along the entire length, except by being villous on the principal veins (vs. adaxially pilosous) and female tepals with ciliate margins (vs. entire to slightly crenulate).
bibliographic_Citation: Jacques E.d.L. 2020, Begonia fimbritepala (Begoniaceae), a new species endemic to the Atlantic Coastal Forest in the state of Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, Phytotaxa. Vol.439(1) , pp.102-106 (https://doi.org/10.11646/phytotaxa.439.1.8)

description: Begonia itingae is most similar to B. organensis Brade but differs by having peltate leaves (vs. basifixed) and a larger membranous ring at the apex of the petiole (4–5 mm long vs. 1–2 mm)Taxonomic notes:—By the presence of a membranous ring at the petiole apex, Begonia itingae resembles B. caraguatatubensis Brade (which is endemic to São Paulo State) as well as B. collaris Brade and B. organensis Brade (which are endemic to Rio de Janeiro State); for additional commentaries on B. collaris, refer to Jacques (1996). Begonia itingae is similar to B. organensis in having stipules that are large, scarious, and persistent, the abaxial surface of the leaf blade with sparse scale-like trichomes on the largest veins, placentae bilamellate, and similar fruits. Begonia organensis, however, has basifixed leaves (vs. peltate) and smaller membranous rings on the petiole apex 1–2 mm (vs. 4–5 mm). Begonia caraguatatubensis and B. collaris have caducous stipules, smaller capsules, with rounded wings and entire placentae.
bibliographic_Citation: Jacques E.d.L. 2018, Four New Brazilian species of Begonia (Begoniaceae), Phytotaxa. Vol.381(1) , pp.86-94 (https://doi.org/10.11646/phytotaxa.381.1.11)

description: Begonia mamedeana is most similar to B. stenophylla A. DC. although differing by having fruits that are larger (1.5–2 cm vs. 0.7–1.1 cm long.), oblong (vs. oblong to oval), with equal wings (vs. unequal) and a tomentose indumentum (vs. villous).
bibliographic_Citation: Jacques E.d.L. 2018, Four New Brazilian species of Begonia (Begoniaceae), Phytotaxa. Vol.381(1) , pp.86-94 (https://doi.org/10.11646/phytotaxa.381.1.11)

description: Begonia rivularis is most similar to B. quetamensis L.B. Sm.& B.G. Schub., although differs by having smaller male tepals 7–14 mm long (vs. 17 mm long.) and styles bifurcate (vs. multifidis).Taxonomic notes: Begonia rivularis is most similar to Begonia quetamensis L.B. Sm.& B.G. Schub. and B. novogranatae A. DC., although it differs from Begonia quetamensis by having smaller male tepals 7–14 mm long (vs. 17 mm long.) and styles bifurcate (vs. multifidis) and from B. novogranatae by having basifixed leaves (vs. peltate), stigmas with bifid branches (vs. multifids) and larger capsules 10–15 (–23) × 25–29 (–40) mm (vs. 8–10 × 10–12 mm).
bibliographic_Citation: Jacques E.d.L. 2018, Four New Brazilian species of Begonia (Begoniaceae), Phytotaxa. Vol.381(1) , pp.86-94 (https://doi.org/10.11646/phytotaxa.381.1.11)

description: Begonia tripicoensis is most similar to B. bidentata Raddi although it can be distinguished by having leaf blades with margins serratedenticulate (vs. bi-dentate), larger, pubescent stipules (1.3–2.4 cm long vs. 0.4–0,9 (–1.3) cm long, glabrous) and round capsules (vs. obovate).Taxonomic notes:—Begonia tripicoensis can be easily recognized by having internodes pubescent, stipules caducous, 20–24 mm long, pubescent, petioles very short, 0.1–0.5 cm, blades 7.3–10.5(–11.5) × 3–4.5 cm, with leaf margins serrate–denticulate, apex acuminate, principal and secondary veins on the adaxial surface little evident, pubescent on the abaxial surface, capsules round, 7–9 mm long. The new species is similar to B. dentatiloba and B. bidentata, and can sometimes grow very near to them. Begonia tripicoensis, however, is easily distinguished from B. dentatiloba as the latter is a more robust plant, with stipules persistent, blades larger, 12–12.5 cm long, principal and secondary veins on the adaxial surface evident, prominent, and capsules larger (10–13 mm long), oblong. Begonia bidentata has internodes puberulous to glabrescent, stipules smaller (0.4–0.9(–1.3) cm long), glabrous, blades with margins bi-dentate, principal and secondary veins evident, deep, and capsules larger (ca. 13 mm long), obovate, with apex truncate.
bibliographic_Citation: Jacques E.d.L. 2018, Four New Brazilian species of Begonia (Begoniaceae), Phytotaxa. Vol.381(1) , pp.86-94 (https://doi.org/10.11646/phytotaxa.381.1.11)

description: This species differs from B. itatinensis by leaf blades 49−65 × 10−15 mm [vs. 10−30(−43) × 5−10 mm], with serrate (vs. deeply serrate) margins, and elliptical (vs. narrowly triangular) stipules 12−22 × 2.5−5 mm (vs. 4−10 × 0.8−2 mm).Taxonomic comments:—Begonia trevisoensis resembles B. itatinensis Irmsch. ex Brade (1944: 15) because both are subshrubs (Figs. 2A, 3A), with symmetric or slightly asymmetric leaf blades at the base (Fig. 2B) and inflorescences with one flower at a time (Figs. 2A, 3B−C). However, B. trevisoensis differs from B. itatinensis by its larger leaf blades 49−65 × 10−15 mm [vs. 10−30(−43) × 5−10 mm], with serrate margins (vs. deeply serrate), and its elliptical (vs. narrowly triangular) stipules, reaching 12−22 × 2.5−5 mm (vs. 4−10 × 0.8−2 mm). It also resembles B. polyandra Irmsch. (1953: 43) due to similar size and shape of its leaves, but B. trevisoensis can be easily distinguished by its one-flowered inflorescences (vs. multi-flowered inflorescences), its elliptic (vs. narrowly triangular) stipules reaching 12−22 × 2.5−5 mm (vs. 5−11 × 2−2.5 mm). Moreover, while B. trevisoensis is endemic from Treviso, in Southeastern Santa Catarina, B. polyandra is only known from the states of São Paulo, Paraná and Northern Santa Catarina. According to its morphological characteristics, including its female flowers with 4 or more perianth segments, its 3-locular ovary with a single placental branch per locule and ellipsoid seeds, 1.7−2.6 times as long as broad, Begonia trevisoensis can be assigned to Begonia sect. Pritzelia (Klotzsch) A. DC., the largest and most morphologically variable section of Neotropical Begonia, whose species are predominantly found in extra-Amazonian Brazil (Doorenbos et al. 1998, Moonlight et al. 2018).
contributor: Jaramillo J.C., Kollmann L.J.C. & Fiaschi P.
bibliographic_Citation: Jaramillo J.C., Kollmann L.J.C. & Fiaschi P. 2018, Begonia trevisoensis, a new species of Begonia sect. Pritzelia (Begoniaceae) from Santa Catarina State, Brazil, Phytotaxa. Vol.381(1) , pp.51-57 (https://doi.org/10.11646/phytotaxa.381.1.8)

description: Begonia langenbergiana is closely related to B. itaguassuensis in its rhizomatous habit, its indumentum of simple trichomes, its reniform, apiculate leaves, its dichotomous inflorescence with persistent bracts and 2 prophylles on pistillate flowers, but can be distinguished by its bullate leaves with adaxially introse and abaxially prominent veins. Furthremore, its first flowers are erect and open when the inflorescence is small and still growing, until his maturity; and the first ramifications of the inflorescences are erect when the inflorescence is growing and until his maturity, and its stigma is without a stigmatic band.Taxonomical notes.—Begonia langenbergiana is closely related to B. itaguassuensis but differs by the lightly bullate leaves (vs. not bullate) with adaxially introse and abaxially prominent veins (vs. veins not adaxially introse and not abaxially prominent); the first flowers are erect and open when the inflorescence is small and still growing, until his maturity (vs. first flowers reflex and open when the inflorescence has just grown); the first ramifications of the inflorescences are erect when the inflorescence is growing until his maturity (vs. first ramifications of the inflorescences are reflex when the inflorescence is growing and erect at maturity); and its stigma are without a stigmatic band (vs. with a stigmatic band). According to the sectional classification of Doorenbos et al. (1998) and Moonlight et al. (2018), B. langenbergiana belongs to Begonia section Pritzelia, which includes approximately 130 species from south America characterized by their entire placentae and the presence of cystoliths in the leaf cells.
bibliographic_Citation: Kollmann L.J.C. 2018, Begonia langenbergiana (Begoniaceae) a new species from the south of São Paulo State, Brazil, Phytotaxa. Vol.381(1) , pp.80-85 (https://doi.org/10.11646/phytotaxa.381.1.10)

description: Begonia itaipeensis is most similar to B. friburgensis Brade but differs in having female flowers with three tepals (vs. five) and a squamulose indumentum (vs. lanate).Taxonomic notes:—Begonia itaipeensis can be easily recognized by its large pistillate flowers up to 20 mm long, with three tepals, and with 1–2 diminute structures on the outside of the tepals, ca. 1mm long, probably glandular. This species resembles B. friburgensis (1957: 31) in its rupicolous habit, leaves with long petioles, up to 15 cm long, and transversely ovate leaf blades, but B. itaipeensis is easily distinguished by its larger blades, 17–27.5 × 10–18 cm (vs. 8–12 ×12–16 cm), with abaxial surface with 2–5-branched trichomes, sparsely distributed, and squamulose (vs. long, intertwined, stellate trichomes, lanate-tomentose), external tepals of male flowers broadly elliptic (vs. oblongtriangular), and three tepals in the pistillate flower (vs. five). The three tepals in the pistillate flower is remarkably rare in Brazilian Begonia species, shared only by five epiphitic species. As delimited by Doorenbos et al. (1998) and Moonlight et al. (2018) all of them belong to B. sect. Trachelocarpus (Müll.Berol) A.DC (B. depauperata Schott (1827: 408), B. fulvo-setulosa Brade (1943: 22), B. herbacea Vell. (1831: 53), B. lanceolata Vell. (1831: 33) and B. velloziana Walp. (1843: 216). The sectional placement of B. itaipeensis is not clear. Although it has some resemblance to B. friburgensis in Begonia sect. Pritzelia, it is abberant for that section in lacking cystoliths and have 3 tepals in the female flowers, and so is considered unplaced to section.
bibliographic_Citation: Jacques E.d.L. 2019, Begonia itaipeensis (Begoniaceae), a new species endemic to Atlantic Coastal Forest in the state of Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, Phytotaxa. Vol.425(1) , pp.57-62 (https://doi.org/10.11646/phytotaxa.425.1.5)

description: This species resembles Begonia lasioura D.C.Thomas& Ardi (Thomas et al. 2011: 233) in the erect habit, the dense indumentum of relatively long (to ca. 2 mm) hairs of the stems and leaves, and the short peduncles of the female inflorescences, but differs by its lower growth habit up to 30 cm tall (vs up to 60 cm tall); a biserrate to shallowly lobed leaf margin (vs leaf margin serrate); and obovate female flower tepals (vs tepals ovate to elliptic).Notes:—Begonia medicinalis differs from B. lasioura as discussed in the diagnosis. There are a few other species with a similarly dense indumentum of relatively long hairs on the vegetative parts such as B. chiasmogyna M.Hughes (2006: 193), B. gambutensis Ardi& D.C.Thomas (Ardi et al. 2014: 260) and B. prionota D.C.Thomas& Ardi (Thomas et al. 2011: 237), but B. medicinalis can be easily distinguished from these species by several characters (see Table 1).
contributor: Ardi W.H., Zubair M.S., Ramadanil & Thomas D.C.
bibliographic_Citation: Ardi W.H., Zubair M.S., Ramadanil & Thomas D.C. 2019, Begonia medicinalis (Begoniaceae), a new species from Sulawesi, Indonesia, Phytotaxa. Vol.423(1) , pp.41-45 (https://doi.org/10.11646/phytotaxa.423.1.5)

description: Begonia cunhambebii is most similar to B. friburgensis Brade but differs by lanate indumentum (vs. lanuginose), bracteoles 2, widely ovate, overlapping each other at the base of the ovary (vs. bracteole 1, linear, not overlapping at base of the ovary) and by male flowers with ovate outer tepals (vs. oblong-triangular).Taxonomic notes:—Begonia cunhambebii can be easily recognized by having very long petioles, 18–40 cm long, half-terete, transversely ovate blades, 19–30 × 14–23 cm, abaxially lanate, ferruginous, with adpressed stellate trichomes (3–5-branched), densely distributed on the primary veins, lobes of blades overlapping the petiole, inflorescence a 6-branched cyme, male flowers with ovate external tepals, with obtuse to rounded apex, female flowers with two bracteoles, widely ovate, overlapping for each other at the base of the ovary, fruits with the largest wing rounded. Begonia cunhambebii is similar to B. friburgensis Brade (1957: 31) and B. fluminensis Brade (1945: 30) which share a repent habit on rocky slopes and outcrops in different areas of Atlantic forest (Brade 1945, 1957), shape of leaves and stellate trichomes. B. cunhambebii resembles B. fluminensis due the lanate indumentum, cordate leaf base, male flowers with ovate external tepals, with obtuse to rounded apex and fruits with the largest wing rounded at apex. B. fluminensis, however, is different because it is a delicate herb (vs. robust) and the lobes of leaves are not overlapping at the petiole (vs. lobes overlapping the petiole). B. cunhambebii resembles B. friburgensis by lobes of blades overlapping the petiole, but B. friburgensis has lanuginose indumentum (vs. lanate, ferruginous), male flowers with oblong-triangular external tepals (vs. ovate), with acuminate apex (vs. obtuse to rounded), and fruits with the largest wing acute at apex (vs. rounded).
bibliographic_Citation: Jacques E.d.L. 2020, Two new Brazilian species of Begonia (Begoniaceae) from Atlantic Coastal Forest , Phytotaxa. Vol.432(1) , pp.38-46 (https://doi.org/10.11646/phytotaxa.432.1.4)

description: Begonia lorenzii is most similar to B. windischii L.B.Sm. ex S.F.Sm.& Wassh. but differs by stems with villous indumentum (vs. glabrous), triangular stipules, ca. 1–1.5 × 0.5 cm (vs. ovate, 2–3 × 1–2 cm) and leaves with ciliate margins (vs. crenate).Taxonomic notes:—Begonia lorenzii can be easily recognized by having villous stems, leaf blades slightly lobate, transversely ovate, 10.5–15 × 5.5–6.5 cm, villous on both surfaces, ciliate at the margin, few-flowered inflorescence, 2-branched cyme, female flowers with one, persistent, inconspicuous bracteole, pistillate flowers with three tepals and capsule sparsely villous, truncate at the apex. Begonia lorenzii resembles B. windischii Smith et al. (1999: 27), which is endemic to São Paulo state, by the shape of the leaves, inflorescence with few flowers, three tepals in the pistillate flowers and shape of capsulae, however B. windishii is a rupicolous herb (vs. terrestrial), with a repent, glabrous stem (vs. erect, villous), leaves with crenate margins (vs. ciliate), with prominent veins and larger stipules 2–3 × 1–2 cm (vs. 1–1.5 × 0.5 cm).
bibliographic_Citation: Jacques E.d.L. 2020, Two new Brazilian species of Begonia (Begoniaceae) from Atlantic Coastal Forest , Phytotaxa. Vol.432(1) , pp.38-46 (https://doi.org/10.11646/phytotaxa.432.1.4)

description: Begonia ehuangzhangensis is most similar to B. fimbristipula Hance (1883: 202) in tuber shape, placentation type, and leaf number, but significantly differs by petiole and blade glabrous (vs. hairy), female flower 2 tepals (vs. 3 tepals), and later flowering period (August vs. May). Begonia ehuangzhangensis also resembles B. rongjiangensis T.C. Ku in Wu& Ku (1995: 279) but distinguished from the latter in having glabrous outer tepals of male flower, glabrous ovary, glabrous and persistent bracts, U-shaped stigmas, and solitary leaf per tuber. Comparison of the above three species is provided in Table 1.NOTE: According to Shui et al. (2002), the most important diagnostic characters for delimiting Begonia sections are the characters of fruits and placentation. Morphologically, B. ehuangzhangensis characterized by having capsulas, placentation axile and bifid, ovary 3-locular, flowers many, and fruit wall hard , can be assigned into B. sect. Diploclinium (Lindl. 1847: 319) A. DC. (1859: 129).
bibliographic_Citation: Ding Q.L. et al. 2018, Begonia ehuangzhangensis (sect. Diploclinium, Begoniaceae), a new species from Guangdong, China, Phytotaxa. Vol.381(1) , pp.107-115 (https://doi.org/10.11646/phytotaxa.381.1.14)

description: Begonia dracopelta with strongly bullate leaf texture most closely resembles like B. dinosauria C.W.Lin& C.-I Peng (2017: 223) from Sarawak, but it can be easily differentiated by its glabrous erect stem, elliptic leaf glabrous on upper surface, male flower with 20–23 stamens, female flower with a longer pedicel (10–17 mm) and ovary glabrescent or with a microscopic indumentum. In contrast, in B. Dinosuaria, the stem is creeping and densely hairy, leaf broadly ovate to reniform and adaxially hairy (the tip of bulla), male flower with 30–40 stamens, female flower pedicel ca. 3–5 mm and ovary with red bristles.Notes:—Strongly bullate leaves are a rare character in Bornean Begonia, also found in B. ruthiae S.Julia (Yun et al., 2015: 75); however that species has pointed bullae, each tipped with a bristle, whilst those of B. dracopelta are glabrous.
contributor: Ardi W.H., Girmansyah D., Lin C-W. & Hughes M.
bibliographic_Citation: Ardi W.H., Girmansyah D., Lin C-W. & Hughes M. 2019, Two new species of Begonia (Begoniaceae) from Borneo, Phytotaxa. Vol.407(1) , pp.22-28 (https://doi.org/10.11646/phytotaxa.407.1.4)

description: Resembling Begonia crockerensis S.Julia (2014: 8) in the creeping habit and leaf shape, but differs by ovate (not lanceolate) and smaller stipules (9–10 × 4.5–5 mm; not 14–23 × 5–7 mm), red bristles between the veins on the leaf adaxial surface (not glabrous); inflorescence protandous (not protogynous), shorter peduncles (5–15 mm, not 2.7–6.5 cm), smaller bracts (5–10 × 3–9 mm, not 10–12 × 6–7 mm) with a serrulate margin (not entire); and fruit wing margins ciliate (not entire).Notes:—Begonia inggitae is allied to B. crockerensis, B. bosuangiana S.Julia (Repin et al. 2015: 6) and B. humericola Sands (2001: 156). Comparison between the most similar species is listed in Table 2.
contributor: Ardi W.H., Girmansyah D., Lin C-W. & Hughes M.
bibliographic_Citation: Ardi W.H., Girmansyah D., Lin C-W. & Hughes M. 2019, Two new species of Begonia (Begoniaceae) from Borneo, Phytotaxa. Vol.407(1) , pp.22-28 (https://doi.org/10.11646/phytotaxa.407.1.4)

description: Notes: Begonia qingchengshanensis resembles B. wilsonii Gagnep., also a member of sect. Reichenheimia occurring in Sichuan, in the widely ovate leaves and 3-locular ovary, each locule with unilamellate placenta. The new species differs from B. wilsonii in having an erect stem (vs. stemless with basal leaves) and ovary trigonous-ellipsoid with 3 wings (vs. clavate and without wings).
contributor: Li H-Z., Guan K-Y., Lin C-W. & Peng C-I.
bibliographic_Citation: Li H-Z., Guan K-Y., Lin C-W. & Peng C-I. 2018, Begonia qingchengshanensis (sect. Reichenheimia, Begoniaceae), a new species from Sichuan, China, Phytotaxa. Vol.349(2) , pp.197-200 (https://doi.org/10.11646/phytotaxa.349.2.12)

description: Begonia palemlemensis resembles B. droseroides in having broadly ovate leaves, glandular hairy pedicels, 4-tepaled staminate flowers, 5-tepaled pistillate flowers with 3-locular ovaries with unequal wings. However, B. palemlemensis differs in the indumentum of the petiole and lamina, which are completely covered with densely erect pilose trichomes (vs. the petiole with densely pale brown, appressed sericeous trichomes, and the lamina above glabrous and with red puberulous trichomes on the lower veins); its denticulate and irregularly lobed laminal margin (vs. subentire, slightly scalloped), acute leaf apex (vs. obtuse to rounded); peduncle with pilose hairs (vs. with glandular hairs) and glandular hairy pedicel, tepals and ovary (vs. completely glabrous).
contributor: Calaramo M.A., Rubite R.R., Pugal C.M. & Lin C-W.
bibliographic_Citation: Calaramo M.A., Rubite R.R., Pugal C.M. & Lin C-W. 2019, New Species of Begonia section Baryandra (Begoniaceae) from Northwestern Luzon, Philippines, Phytotaxa. Vol.407(1) , pp.36-42 (https://doi.org/10.11646/phytotaxa.407.1.6)

description: It is similar to B. labordei Lév. (1904: 323), sharing staminate and pistillate flowers with four tepals, but differs in its lanceolate leaves (vs broadly ovate), largest fruit wing falciform with superior margin ascending (vs triangular, superior margin horizontal).Discussion:—Among Chinese Begonia, there are three species that have lanceolate leaves with cuneate bases. Two species, B. yingjiangensis S.H.Huang (1999: 18) and B. rongjiangensis T.C.Ku (1995: 279) belong to Begonia sect. Platycentrum (Klotzsch 1855: 123) de Candolle (1859: 134), and the third one, viz. the new species proposed here, belongs to Sect. Diploclinium (Lindl. 1846: 319) de Candolle (1859: 129). The new species belongs in Begonia sect. Diploclinium due to its tuberous habit and bifid axile placentae. The new species is also similar to B. xingyiensis T.C.Ku (1995: 263) in its stemless and tuberous habit, and staminate and pistillate flowers with four tepals, but differs in its strigose lanceolate leaves with a cuneate base (vs sparsely villous, broadly ovate with a cordate base). Finally, the new species is also similar to B. gigabracteata H.Z. Li& H. Ma (2008: 157) in its stemless and tuberous habit, staminate flowers with four tepals but differs in its lanceolate leaves (vs slightly oblique, obovate), lamina abaxially sparsely strigose (vs both sides glabrous), pistillate flowers with four tepals (vs with 5 tepals).
bibliographic_Citation: He S.Z. et al. 2019, A new species of Begonia Linn. (Begoniaceae) in karst regions from Guizhou, China, Phytotaxa. Vol.409(1) , pp.49-52 (https://doi.org/10.11646/phytotaxa.409.1.7)

description: The new species is similar to Begonia hahiepiana H.Q.Nguyen& Tebbitt in its habit, leaf morphology and 3-loculed ovary, but differs principally in its cylindrical petiole (vs grooved), pistillate flower with obovate outer petals and lanceolate inner petals (vs with broadly oblong outer and inner petals), and fruit trigonous-ellipsoid (vs trigonous-spherical) and ratio of length to width 2.9‒3.4 (vs 1.1‒1.2).
bibliographic_Citation: Chen W.H., et al. 2020, Two new baccate species of Begonia sect. Platycentrum (Begoniaceae) from Vietnam, Phytotaxa. Vol.443(1) , pp.92-100 (https://dx.doi.org/10.11646/phytotaxa.443.1.8)

description: It is most similar to Begonia kasutensis K.G.Pearce (2003: 82) from Niah National Park, Sarawak in its glabrous leaves with laminas as broad as long with two main veins and an additional two veins in the basal lobe; however, B. apiensis is different in its petioles that are more-or-less the length of lamina, its plain green and smaller lamina 2.2– 3.5 × 2.2–4 cm with an almost entire margin, whereas B. kasutensis has a petiole less than half the length of lamina, the lamina is variegated and is larger, 4.7–6.2 × 3.9–5.5 cm, and the margin is irregularly serrulate.Notes:—It is a unique limestone species because it grows at high elevation in lower montane forest above 800 m. It is a decorative species in its tiny rounded leaves and low often creeping habit.
contributor: Sang J., Kiew R. & Geri C.
bibliographic_Citation: Sang J., Kiew R. & Geri C. 2013, Revision of Begonia (Begoniaceae) from the Melinau Limestone in Gunung Mulu National Park and Gunung Buda National Park, Sarawak, Borneo, including thirteen new species, Phytotaxa. Vol.99(1) , pp.1-34 (http://dx.doi.org/10.11646/phytotaxa.99.1.1)

description: Notes:—It is a decorative species often with a creeping habit and rooting at the nodes. Its leaves are tiny, 2.2–3.5 × 2.2–4 cm, rather stiff, dark green, glabrous, rounded or ovate, more or less equal-sided, scarcely oblique with large ovate stipules to 3.5 cm × 2.5 cm. Its fruit pedicel is pendent and 15–25 mm long.
contributor: Sang J., Kiew R. & Yiing L.C.
bibliographic_Citation: Sang J., Kiew R. & Yiing L.C. 2018, The Begonia flora of Gunung Mulu and Gunung Buda National Parks, Sarawak, Borneo, including five new species, Phytotaxa. Vol.381(1) , pp.058-079 (https://doi.org/10.11646/phytotaxa.381.1.9)

description: It is most similar to Begonia apiensis Kiew& S.Julia in its small, glabrous leaves with the lamina as broad as long, in its two main veins with a further two in the basal lobe, in its petiole more-or-less the length of lamina, and the entire margin but B. benaratensis is different from B. apiensis in its creeping habit, larger stipules ca. 5 × 3 mm (not ca. 3 × 2.5 mm), ovate or rounded lamina (not reniform), bigger bracts ca. 5 × 3 mm (not ca. 4 × 2 mm), much larger tepals in female flower 8–10 × 3–8 mm (not 2–2.5 × 1–1.5 mm), larger male flowers ca. 8 × 8 mm (not 4.5–5.5 × 4 mm), number of stamens 25–30 (not 15–20) and narrower fruits ca. 12 × 5 mm (not 10–18 × 6–19 mm).Notes:—The species is most similar to B. apiensis but the habitat is completely different. It grows on lightly shaded mossy rock faces below 300 m compared with B. apiensis that is only found above 800 m. Found in localized patches, B. benaratensis sometimes grows together with B. rhodoneura that is more widespread.
contributor: Sang J., Kiew R. & Geri C.
bibliographic_Citation: Sang J., Kiew R. & Geri C. 2013, Revision of Begonia (Begoniaceae) from the Melinau Limestone in Gunung Mulu National Park and Gunung Buda National Park, Sarawak, Borneo, including thirteen new species, Phytotaxa. Vol.99(1) , pp.1-34 (http://dx.doi.org/10.11646/phytotaxa.99.1.1)

description: Notes:—A creeping species, rooting at the nodes with slender stems and small plain green leaves, 1.5–4 × 2.2–5 cm. The whole plant is glabrous. The fruit pedicel is ca. 15 mm long and pendent. At the Botanical Research Centre, Semenggoh, Sarawak, plant material collected from Gunung Benarat that was planted in pocket of soils on a concrete wall grew well and now flower throughout the year.
contributor: Sang J., Kiew R. & Yiing L.C.
bibliographic_Citation: Sang J., Kiew R. & Yiing L.C. 2018, The Begonia flora of Gunung Mulu and Gunung Buda National Parks, Sarawak, Borneo, including five new species, Phytotaxa. Vol.381(1) , pp.058-079 (https://doi.org/10.11646/phytotaxa.381.1.9)

description: Notes:—In its small variegated leaves and creeping habit, it is as Low noted on his specimen ‘a charming plant’. The fruit is interesting in that one locule is hardly developed (it is about a quarter the size of the other two). A similar situation is seen in B. amphioxus Sands (1990: 77) (Kiew 2001).
contributor: Sang J., Kiew R. & Geri C.
bibliographic_Citation: Sang J., Kiew R. & Geri C. 2013, Revision of Begonia (Begoniaceae) from the Melinau Limestone in Gunung Mulu National Park and Gunung Buda National Park, Sarawak, Borneo, including thirteen new species, Phytotaxa. Vol.99(1) , pp.1-34 (http://dx.doi.org/10.11646/phytotaxa.99.1.1)

description: Notes:—A very attractive species with small variegated leaves and creeping habit rooting at the nodes, its leaves are covered on the upper leaf surface by stiff hairs each raised on a small cone that give the leaf its rough surface. Leaves vary in colour from dark green or blackish purple above to pale green with dark green veins above. Its 2-tepaled male flower is sparsely hispid.
contributor: Sang J., Kiew R. & Yiing L.C.
bibliographic_Citation: Sang J., Kiew R. & Yiing L.C. 2018, The Begonia flora of Gunung Mulu and Gunung Buda National Parks, Sarawak, Borneo, including five new species, Phytotaxa. Vol.381(1) , pp.058-079 (https://doi.org/10.11646/phytotaxa.381.1.9)

description: Begonia conniegeriae is similar to B. congesta Ridley (1906: 253) from the Bau limestone in Kuching Division, in its leaves that are neither hairy nor appear velvety and in its distantly toothed leaf margin, but it is distinct from B. congesta in its glossy leaves, its larger elliptic male tepals ca. 7 × 3 mm (not rotund and 4–5 × 4–5 mm) on longer pedicals 8–10 mm (not 5–7 mm long) and in its shorter fruits 20–22 mm (not ca. 25 mm long) and oblong fruits (not almost square in outline).Notes:—This species belongs to a group of begonias that has apparently diversified on limestone hills. The first to be described was B. congesta Ridley from the Bau limestone, Kuching Division (Ridley 1906). In Mulu three species occur, B. conniegeriae, B. melinauensis and B. umbratica. They are erect shrubby begonias characterized by their thick stems often swollen nodes, the narrowly bifurcating veins that give the leaf surface a corrugate appearance, the often congested basal branches of the inflorescence and the many tiny flowers. In the field each species is distinctive but some characters, for examples, velvety appearance of the lamina (B. melinauensis and B. umbratica) or the orientation of the leaf (B. melinauensis) are lost on pressing and drying. This species is a case in point because its glossy leaves so conspicuous in the field separate it from the other species in this group.
contributor: Sang J., Kiew R. & Geri C.
bibliographic_Citation: Sang J., Kiew R. & Geri C. 2013, Revision of Begonia (Begoniaceae) from the Melinau Limestone in Gunung Mulu National Park and Gunung Buda National Park, Sarawak, Borneo, including thirteen new species, Phytotaxa. Vol.99(1) , pp.1-34 (http://dx.doi.org/10.11646/phytotaxa.99.1.1)

description: Notes:—A shrubby species with thick stems 2–3 mm when dried, often with swollen nodes and glossy leaves (in life) held horizontally with a corrugated surface with bifurcating palmate veins arranged closely together. The lamina is as long as wide, oblique, asymmetric and glossy with broad side 7.5–12 cm. Its stipule has a distinct midrib, ca. 12 × 3 mm and is caducous. It has congested inflorescences shorter than the petioles with bracts to 14 × 7 mm.
contributor: Sang J., Kiew R. & Yiing L.C.
bibliographic_Citation: Sang J., Kiew R. & Yiing L.C. 2018, The Begonia flora of Gunung Mulu and Gunung Buda National Parks, Sarawak, Borneo, including five new species, Phytotaxa. Vol.381(1) , pp.058-079 (https://doi.org/10.11646/phytotaxa.381.1.9)

description: It is similar to Begonia kachak K.G. Pearce (2003: 74) from Niah National Park in its thick rhizome, large and rounded leaves with widely spaced veins and in its inflorescences with one or two pairs of female flowers at the base and a long raceme of male flowers above. It differs from this species in its much larger leaves with a glabrous petiole 9–25 cm long and a lamina 10.5–18.5 × 14–23 cm (compared with a bristly petiole 2–17 cm long and lamina 7.5–12.5 × 7.5–15 cm in B. kachak) and larger capsule 14–23 × 10–16 mm (not ca. 19 × 16 mm).Notes:—This common species shows some differences between populations. For example, plants from Gunung Buda have a more pronounced scalloped margin compared to scarcely toothed margin for plants from Lobang Cina and Sungai Terikan; while those from Clearwater Cave and Bukit Berar have more rounded, less oblique leaves and smaller leaves (ca. 10.5 11 cm) compared to those from Sungai Terikan (15.5–17 × 16– 18.5 cm).
contributor: Sang J., Kiew R. & Geri C.
bibliographic_Citation: Sang J., Kiew R. & Geri C. 2013, Revision of Begonia (Begoniaceae) from the Melinau Limestone in Gunung Mulu National Park and Gunung Buda National Park, Sarawak, Borneo, including thirteen new species, Phytotaxa. Vol.99(1) , pp.1-34 (http://dx.doi.org/10.11646/phytotaxa.99.1.1)

description: Notes:—A creeping or scrambling species, rooting at the nodes with plain green, slightly oblique leaves, 8.5–21 × 12–25 cm, with scalloped or toothed margin. The venation is palmate-pinnate with 3–4 veins in basal lobe.
contributor: Sang J., Kiew R. & Yiing L.C.
bibliographic_Citation: Sang J., Kiew R. & Yiing L.C. 2018, The Begonia flora of Gunung Mulu and Gunung Buda National Parks, Sarawak, Borneo, including five new species, Phytotaxa. Vol.381(1) , pp.058-079 (https://doi.org/10.11646/phytotaxa.381.1.9)

description: In its small size and creeping habit, non-peltate leaves and long inflorescences from the upper leaf axils, it resembles Begonia kasutensis K.G.Pearce from Niah National Park, but from which it can be distinguished by the following characters: longer petiole of the lower leaves 4–8 cm long (not 3.8 cm), the very oblique and much broader lamina 5–10 5–13 cm (not scarcely oblique lamina 4.7–6.2 × 3.9–5.5 cm), the shorter capsule 8–15 × 10–12 mm (not 16 × 12 mm) and stamens numbering 30–46 (not 20).Notes:—This species is common and widespread, creeping on rock faces in lowland limestone forest.
contributor: Sang J., Kiew R. & Geri C.
bibliographic_Citation: Sang J., Kiew R. & Geri C. 2013, Revision of Begonia (Begoniaceae) from the Melinau Limestone in Gunung Mulu National Park and Gunung Buda National Park, Sarawak, Borneo, including thirteen new species, Phytotaxa. Vol.99(1) , pp.1-34 (http://dx.doi.org/10.11646/phytotaxa.99.1.1)

description: Notes:—A creeping species with slender stems often rooting at the nodes, rarely branching. It has plain, glabrous and oblique leaves, 5–10 × 5–13 cm, with deeply cordate but not overlapping leaf base, serrate margin and mucronate leaf apex, palmate venation with 1–2 veins in basal lobe. The inflorescence is longer than petiole, while the capsule is broadly ovate, 8–15 × 9–13 mm.
contributor: Sang J., Kiew R. & Yiing L.C.
bibliographic_Citation: Sang J., Kiew R. & Yiing L.C. 2018, The Begonia flora of Gunung Mulu and Gunung Buda National Parks, Sarawak, Borneo, including five new species, Phytotaxa. Vol.381(1) , pp.058-079 (https://doi.org/10.11646/phytotaxa.381.1.9)

description: It most resembles Begonia stichochaete K.G.Pearce (2003: 78) from Niah National Park but it is different from this species in its more robust habit with stems to 3–5 mm diameter (not 5–9 mm), bristles to 5 mm long (not ca. 2 mm) and internodes 1–1.5 cm long (not 2.5–5 mm) with smaller stipules (ca. 12 × 3 mm not ca. 17 × 11 mm); narrower laminas 10–12.5 × 3.7–4.5 cm (not 11–19 × 7.5–10 cm) with the broad side measuring 2–2.5 cm wide (not 6–7.5 cm) and the basal lobe 3–5 mm long (not 1.7 cm); smaller bracts ca. 3 × 1 mm (not ca. 13 ×10 mm) and uppermost bracts 2 0.5 mm (not 12 × 12 mm). In addition, Begonia stichochaete has erect panicles to 3.4 cm long, whereas in B. magentifolia one, almost sessile, male flower is produced per leaf axil.Notes:—Begonia magentifolia is striking in its hispid stem and petiole and in its dark jade green leaves with red hairs on the upper surface and the rich magenta lower surface. It belongs to a distinct group of begonias in sect. Petermannia that have a short, unbranched stem, very short petioles and non-oblique leaves where the petiole does not form an angle with the midrib. Among this group that includes B. berhamanii Kiew (2001: 254), B. caulifora Sands (1990: 68), B. pubescens Ridley (1906: 254) and B. stichochaete K.G.Pearce, it most resembles Begonia stichochaete from the Subis limestone in the Niah National Park. In Sarawak, this group of species is infrequent on limestone substrates.
contributor: Sang J., Kiew R. & Geri C.

Vol.99(1) , pp.1-34 (http://dx.doi.org/10.11646/phytotaxa.99.1.1)

description: Notes:—A more detailed description is provided together with a figure to show the flowers because more individuals were encountered during the present survey. Two colour forms were observed; one with leaves green above and pale green below; the other bronzy green above and magenta below. In addition, fruit is commonly found with three well-developed wings and three small wings. This is unusual in Bornean Begonia that usually have three wings but it is known from a very few species such as B. hexaptera Sands (1997: 434) from Brunei.
contributor: Sang J., Kiew R. & Yiing L.C.
