description: Notes.— Begonia prolifera is known from a single small population in Kanchanaburi. Its vegetative characters resemble B. fibrosa in some aspects (see notes under B. fibrosa for diagnostic characters). It may be more widely distributed on limestone outcrops along the Tenasserim range, on both the Thai and Myanmar sides. Lack of observations may be due to difficulty of accessing the friable limestone habitat of this species during the wet season, and during the dry season it dies back to a small tuber.

description: Notes.— B. pteridiformis differs from other species in sect. Lauchea in having many (8-30) narrowly lanceolate leaves held on horizontal stems. This makes it appear, at first glance, like a pinnately compound fern leaf. The specific epithet ‘pteridiformis’ is derived from this characteristic leaf arrangement.

description: Notes.— Begonia pumila is known only from an isolated inselberg, the type locality at Khao Pho Ta Chong Dong, Ranong province. The conservation status of this species needs further evaluation in the field.

description: Notes.— Craib (1931) described Begonia sibthorpioides Ridl. var. grandifolia Craib from the same locality as B. pumilio Irmsch. There is no doubt that both names belong to the same taxon. Begonia pumilio is known only from karst limestone in Phangnga province; further exploration along this karst range into northern Peninsular Malaysia could potentially reveal further records.

description: Notes.— Begonia putii is a very rare species, found only in the north of the Tenasserim range in Chiang Mai province and continuing to the Tanon Thongchai range in Tak province, where it is restricted to exposed limestone, an unusual habitat for Thai begonias. The ovary of this species is unique in having long pilose hairs.

description: Begonia egamii D. Borah, Taram& M. Hughes has a very unusual combination of characters, making it hard to find a close ally for taxonomic comparison. It shares some characters with B. tamdaoensis C.I Peng such as having hispid hairs on the tepals and ovary and a zygomorphic androecium, but differs in having leaves rugulose above (vs. smooth), two stigmas (vs. three), and anthers retuse at the apex (vs. with an extended connective).
contributor: Borah D., Taram M. & Hughes M.
bibliographic_Citation: Borah D., Taram M. & Hughes M. 2023, Begonia egamii (Begoniaceae), a remarkable new species from Arunachal Pradesh, India, Candollea. Vol.78(2) , pp.147-151 (https://doi.org/10.15553/c2023v782a5)

description: Similar to B. circumlobata, B. jinyuensis and B. scitifolia in having deeply palmately lobed leaves. Begonia ziroensis differs from B. circumlobata and B. jinyuensis in having the main two leaf lobes sharing a main vein at the base (not all leaf lobes with a distinct main vein not shared with other lobes), and capsules covered with very dense short fleshy hairs (not glabrous). It differs from B. scitifolia in having the main two leaf lobes sharing a main vein at the base (not all leaf lobes with a distinct main vein not shared with other lobes), leaf lobes which are broader and deeply and broadly dentate (not dentate), and capsules which are covered with very dense short fleshy hairs (not minutely pilose).
bibliographic_Citation: 2024, A new species Begonia ziroensis and a new record of Begonia siamensis from Arunachal Pradesh, Northeast India, N. Z. J. Bot (https://doi.org/10.1080/0028825X.2023.2295439)

description: Begonia merendonensis Moonlight& D. L. Kelly differs from B. assurgens Irmsch. in its staminate flowers with four (vs. two) tepals and 25 to 30 (vs. 13 to 20) stamens and its pistillate flowers with three (vs. two) tepals, three (vs. two) styles, and villous (vs. glabrous to sparsely pilose) ovary and wings.Within its range, Begonia merendonensis is a highly distinctive species. The only two other members of Begonia sect. Gireoudia known from Cortés Department are B. plebeja Liebm. and B. sericoneura Liebm., which both have thickened rhizomes with short (< 5 mm long) internodes that contrast with the narrow, elongated ( 2 cm long) internodes of B. merendonensis. Other species known from Cortés Department can be easily distinguished because they do not root at the nodes.In the key to the Begonia species of Mesoamerica provided by Burt-Utley (2015), B. merendonensis keys out as B. assurgens at couplet 135 of key 6 (couplet 131 in the PDF version). Both species are recognized by their glabrous to sparsely pubescent, elongated rhizomes and transversely ovate leaves held on elongated (up to 32 cm long) petioles. Distinguishing these two species when sterile is difficult, but in flower they are distinguished with ease by the number of tepals on their staminate (four in B. merendonensis, two in B. assurgens) and pistillate (three in B. merendonensis, two in B. assurgens) flowers.
bibliographic_Citation: Moonlight P.W. & Kelly D.L. 2024, Two New Critically Endangered Species of Begonia sect. Gireoudia (Begoniaceae) from Mesoamerica, Novon. Vol.32.

description: Begonia multiloba Moonlight differs from B. almedana Burt-Utley& Utley in its leaves which have 5 to 9 narrowly acuminate lobes around the margin (vs. 3 to 5 lobes, the lobes broadly triangular) and conspicuously dentate, ciliate margins (vs. serrulate to denticulate, sparsely ciliate); its caducous, membranaceous, broadly ovate bracts (vs. persistent, chartaceous, and narrowly lanceolate); and its staminate flowers with 2 or 3 (vs. 4) tepals and ca. 25 (vs. 30 to 75) stamens.Begonia multiloba is the only species in Guatemala with elongate rhizomes and broadly ovate leaves. Two specimens of this species (Ávila et al. 3288 and Quezada 1767) were previously identified as B. crassicaulis Lindl, which is also a species with multilobed leaves from which B. multiloba is easily differentiated by its < 1 cm thick rhizomes with elongate internodes to at least 8 cm (vs. rhizomes 1–3 cm thick, with internodes only reaching 2.5 cm long) and its straight (vs. sinuous) leaf lobes. The third specimen (Quezada 1819) was previously identified as B. acutiloba Liebm., a poorly known species endemic to Oaxaca State, Mexico (Burt-Utley, 2015).In the key to the begonias of Mesoamericana provided by Burt-Utley (2015), Begonia multiloba keys out as B. mcphersonii Burt-Utley& Utley in couplet 85 of key 5. This species is endemic to Panama and can be distinguished from B. multiloba by its persistent (vs. early deciduous) stipules, its longer leaf lobes (the largest to one third or one half the length of the leaf, versus to one fourth of the length of the leaf), and its densely villous (vs. tomentose to densely tomentose) petioles.
bibliographic_Citation: Moonlight P.W. & Kelly D.L. 2024, Two New Critically Endangered Species of Begonia sect. Gireoudia (Begoniaceae) from Mesoamerica, Novon. Vol.32.

description: Begonia naraharii superficially resembles three other species from Begonia sect. Platycentrum, namely B. lophura Hoang& Lin (2021: 268), B. iridescens Dunn (1920: 110) and B. rockii Irmscher (1939: 544). These four species share several characteristics, including the monoecious rhizomatous herbaceous habit, ovate leaves that produce blue iridescence on the adaxial surface when light is reflected, and 4-tepaled staminate flowers. description: This new species is mostly similar to B. fimbristipula Hance in similar plant size, leaf shape, leaf hairs, and morphology of flowers and fruits, but differs mainly in its thickly unillamelate (vs. thinly bilamellate) placentae of the ovary, later (Jun.–Oct. vs. Apr.–Jun.) flowering time, and smaller flower size (5–11 × 5–10 mm vs. 8–15 × 8–12 mm outer tepals of staminate flower). Begonia ruchengensis belongs to B. sect. Reichenheimia based on its tuberous habit and unilamellate placentae of ovary. It is very difficult to differentiate it from B. fimbristipula without the examination of the ovary placentae. Therefore, they possibly have the closest relationship, which need to be investigated by molecular analysis.

description: The new species is mostly similar to B. villifolia Irmsch. in hairy leaves, flowers and fruits, but is easily differentiated by its 3 (vs. 2) incomplete-locular ovary, concaved (vs. flat) abaxial wing, shorter (to 60 vs. to 100 cm) plant, usually multicolored (vs. pure green) leaf, early (Feb. to Mar. vs. May to Jul.) flowering time. It is also morphologically close to B. khaophanomensis Phutthai& M.Hughes (Phutthai and Hughes, 2016) native to Thailand in the same section, but differs mainly by the latter’s leaf lobed (vs. unlobed), and abaxial wing larger (4 cm vs. ca. 1 cm long), and wing shape (oblong or obliquely triangular vs. auricular).This species usually has two styles and stigmas but three-locular ovary in which two locules are normally developed and the third one is degenerated. It should be placed in B. sect. Platycentrum based on the overall morphology. The new species could be an ideal material for studying the evolution of three locules to two locules of ovary in Begonia.

description: Begonia floriprolifera is morphologically close to B. bonii Gapnep. in the same section, but can be mainly distinguished from the latter by its nearly glabrous (vs. pilose) stipules, short shorter inflorescence (2.5–20 cm vs. over 20 cm), bilaterally symmetric and upward curved (vs. radially symmetric and capitate) androecium, fewer (up to 32 vs. usually over 40) stamens, and anther apex (concave vs. rounded) (Table 1, Fig. S2). Moreover, this species showed rich variation in leaf color (adaxially green to brownish red, abaxially light green to deep red), size and color of variegation patches (absent to large), and flower color (white to pink) (Fig. 2 and 3). In addition, this species is also morphologically similar to B. bamaensis Yan Liu& C.I Peng and B. lui S.M.Ku, C.I Peng& Yan Liu in the same section. However, it differs from B. bamaensis by leaf size and color, indumentums of leaf and flower, stamen number and fruit morphology (Liu et al., 2007). It could be also distinguished from B. lui in plant size, leaf morphology (blade color, leaf maculations, etc.), morphology of flower and fruit, and flowering time (Liu et al., 2020).

description: Begonia barosma morphologically resembles B. lanternaria in rhizome and flower characters. However, it differs from the latter in having fleshy, relatively flat leaf blade which is adaxially blackish-green along main veins, randomly silver white between the veins, abaxailly purple-red and densely pilose along main veins, pale green between the veins. In addition, the new species also can be distinguished from B. lanternaria in sparsely pilose on abaxial surface of outer tepals.

description: Similar to Begonia anisoptera in having obliquely ovate to widely ovate leaves, 4-tepaled staminate and pis-tillate flowers and three winged capsules. However, the new species can be easily distinguished in having stip-ules glabrescent (vs. densely hirsute), petioles 16.5–28.0 cm long, indumentum reddish-maroon, appressed (vs. 4–12 cm long, hairs brown and spreading), larger leaves 8–17 × 7.0–11.5 cm, distantly serrate (vs. 6–12 × 4–8 cm, entire), inflorescence cymosely branching 5–7 times (vs. 2–3 times), oblanceolate inner staminate and pistillate tepals (vs. obovate to cuneiform) with rounded apex (vs. truncate to slightly retuse), capsule recurved or pendu-lous (vs. splash cup), wings subequal and flat (vs. strong-ly unequal, abaxial wing cucullate, lateral wings curved).

description: Begonia abhak resembles B. panayensis Merril in having tall, erect and glabrous stems, oblanceolate leaves, glossy surface adaxially, light green abaxially, acuminate apex, acute base, 2 tepaled staminate flowers, 5 tepaled pistillate flowers and green ovaries with pink wings. However, B. abhak differs in having shorter stems at 1.3 m (vs. 1.5 m), stipules broadly ovate at 19–20 × 9–10 mm (vs. oblanceolate 15–20 mm long), smaller lamina at 14–15 × 5.5–6 cm (vs. 16–20 × 4–6 cm.) with serrated margins (vs. dentate), broadly ovate male tepals (vs. orbicular), shorter and narrower capsules at 16–17 × 14–15 mm. (vs. longer and wider 25 × 20 mm).
